title: Stage timing chronicle — p50/p95/p99 cohort breakdown and microtrace samples
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a running log of a week-long exploratory profiling session focused on end-to-end request latency with explicit per-stage breakdowns and quantiles (p50/p95/p99). Goal: identify high-impact sources of tail latency across different request cohorts (seq-len, kv-hit vs kv-miss, batch-size) and produce concrete mitigations to cut p99 by at least 30% for the problematic cohorts.

What we sampled:
- Timeframe: 2026-02-16 -> 2026-02-19
- Sampled ~18,500 requests across one production cluster (gpu-pool-prod-3) during normal traffic window (09:00–17:00 PST).
- Sampling strata: randomized per-request with bias towards upper-percentile (we oversample requests with latency > p95 in prior week).
- Cohorts defined for breakdowns: 
  1) short (<= 128 tokens) 
  2) mid (129-512 tokens) 
  3) long (> 512 tokens)
  4) cold-kv-miss (first request after model or kv-shard recycle)
  5) warm-kv-hit
- Instrumentation points (timestamps recorded in each request trace): recv, auth, route, preproc, compile/opt, kv-lookup, batch-wait, forward (GPU exec), kv-update, postproc, encode, egress.

Aggregate quantiles (overall cohort summaries):
- Short (N=9,540): overall p50=86ms, p95=220ms, p99=410ms
- Mid (N=6,470): overall p50=150ms, p95=420ms, p99=890ms
- Long (N=1,890): overall p50=420ms, p95=1,200ms, p99=3,100ms
- Cold-kv-miss (N=520): overall p50=310ms, p95=950ms, p99=2,400ms
- Warm-kv-hit (N=16,980): overall p50=120ms, p95=330ms, p99=700ms

Representative per-stage breakout (short cohort, median, p95, p99):
- recv: p50=2ms, p95=6ms, p99=12ms
- auth: p50=1ms, p95=2ms, p99=4ms
- route: p50=3ms, p95=8ms, p99=15ms
- preproc: p50=10ms, p95=28ms, p99=60ms
- compile/opt: p50=6ms, p95=30ms, p99=140ms (note: tail dominated by JIT slow paths)
- kv-lookup: p50=4ms, p95=58ms, p99=320ms (kv-miss amplification)
- batch-wait: p50=20ms, p95=70ms, p99=360ms (head-of-line blocking visible)
- forward (GPU): p50=18ms, p95=34ms, p99=120ms (long seqlen cohorts show much higher)
- kv-update: p50=3ms, p95=10ms, p99=40ms
- postproc: p50=6ms, p95=15ms, p99=30ms
- encode: p50=5ms, p95=12ms, p99=28ms
- egress: p50=2ms, p95=6ms, p99=10ms

Observations and notable patterns:
1) Two distinct tail modes: (A) kv-related tails (kv-lookup and kv-update) where p99 >> p95 and (B) batching wait tails where a small fraction of requests incur large batch-wait delays (head-of-line). Both modes combine to produce most p99 events.
2) compile/opt stage: a cluster of p99 spikes correlates with model-config changes. JIT optimizer fallback paths and trace warmup produce 100–300ms spikes; these are concentrated in requests that hit new model versions or new quantized kernel paths.
3) GPU forward stage contributes strongly for long cohort p99s; however, when normalized per-token, most of the extra latency is GPU compute — expected. The surprising part is variability in CPU->GPU transfer: NVLink bandwidth saturation events correlate with microbursts from large batches.
4) Cold-kv-miss cohort shows kv-lookup median ~60ms and p99 multiple seconds in a subset — those are remote-shard misses that trigger synchronous fetch-from-slow-backend.
5) Batch-wait pathology: requests with small token counts get batched behind a single long request and then wait for the batch to be processed together; p95 for batch-wait is 70ms but p99 is 360ms. Correlates with mixed-seqlen batches where a long request enters the same batch.
6) Network egress and auth are negligible except for a few outliers tied to transient upstream DNS failures (investigate separately).

Microtrace examples (short cohort p99 sample):
- trace-id: s-99123 | recv 3ms | auth 2ms | route 4ms | preproc 12ms | compile 140ms | kv-lookup 320ms | batch-wait 360ms | forward 120ms | postproc 28ms | encode 25ms | egress 8ms | total 1,022ms
- note: this sample shows compounded tails across compile, kv, and batch-wait — not a single root cause.

Hypotheses (ranked by expected impact):
A) Reduce kv tail by adding async fallback + local in-memory bloom-filter to avoid blocking synchronous remote fetches on miss (expected p99 reduction ~25–40% for cold cohort).
B) Improve batching isolation by seqlen-aware batching lanes (e.g., small/large lanes) to avoid long requests delaying small ones. Quick win: separate batch window for short requests (expected p99 reduction ~30% for short cohort).
C) Stabilize compile/opt paths by prewarming kernels at rollout time and avoiding JIT fallback for canary traffic; also add precompiled kernel cache warmup step. (expected p99 reduction for compile tails ~40–60% for affected windows).
D) Add a bounded transfer shaper for GPU host->device to prevent microburst NVLink saturation and prioritize low-latency small requests. (impact moderate; requires kernel/driver tuning).

Short-term experiments to run (next 2 weeks):
1) Feature flag: enable seqlen lane with 2 lanes (short <=128, others) on staging pool and run A/B traffic for 48h. Metric: p99_short and overall p95. Owner: Miguel.
2) Spike: implement async-kv-fallback (return tentative cached token and fetch remote async) on a small customer see if correctness/regression acceptable. Owner: Sanjay.
3) Prewarm: add prewarm job triggered at model rollout that touches most frequent kernel paths for each quantization profile. Owner: Liam.
4) Telemetry: add taggable trace flags for 'kv-shard-origin' and 'batch-content' to quickly slice tail traces. Owner: Anika.

Monitoring KPIs and dashboards to add:
- Per-stage p50/p95/p99 heatmap by cohort (seq-len, kv-hit/miss, batch-size) with rollover latency alerts when any stage p99 exceeds baseline + 2x
- Live scatter of batch-wait vs batch-composition (plot small-request latency in batches containing large requests)
- Kernel-warmth index: fraction of requests hitting precompiled kernels per model-version

Open questions / unknowns:
- Are remote-kv misses due to GC/rebalancing on the kv service or network blips? Need logs from kv-shard owners. Linked ticket: SERV-4021 (contact infra team).
- Does NVLink microburst correlate with noisy-neighbors from other tenants on multi-tenant nodes? Need host-level telemetry.
- Could we legally accept eventual consistency in async-kv for some customers (trade correctness for latency)? Product decision.

Action items (owner / due):
- Miguel: run seqlen-lane A/B on staging (due 2026-02-26)
- Sanjay: prototype async-kv-fallback for internal test customer (due 2026-03-03)
- Liam: enable prewarm on next canary rollout and measure compile-stage p99 (due 2026-03-01)
- Anika: add trace tags and update dashboards for per-stage p99 heatmap (due 2026-02-25)

Notes-to-self (raw):
- keep traces small when sharing with infra (PII) — strip prompt content and replace with length and hash
- remember to check kernel versions on nodes that produced worst p99s (gpu-pool-prod-3-azb)
- compare with last month's baseline: overall p99 short cohort increased by ~12% — likely due to recent rollout that touched kernel selectors

Appendix: quick heuristics used for causal attribution
- if compile/opt > 2x median and correlates with model-version change in trace -> attribute to JIT/compile
- if kv-lookup > 10x median and kv-shard != local -> attribute to remote-fetch; check shard logs
- if batch-wait >> median and batch contains any request > 2x median seqlen -> attribute to batching head-of-line

End of chronicle entry.
(Will append updated A/B results and follow-ups here.)
